keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The definition of 'no-spend' varies widely — some people ban all discretionary spending, others only target specific categories like eating out or shopping. The rules determine the entire structure of the plan.
Whether this is a solo challenge or involves a partner, family, or housemates changes accountability structures, shared expense rules, and how the plan is communicated.
The starting date and any known events (birthdays, travel, social obligations) within the 30 days affect how the plan handles exceptions and high-risk moments.
Fixed financial obligations (rent, subscriptions, bills) must be distinguished from discretionary spending — knowing what is already locked in shapes what 'no-spend' actually covers.
Understanding the underlying goal — saving a target amount, breaking a habit, reducing debt — defines what success looks like and how to measure progress at the end.
Some people need strict rules and daily check-ins; others prefer flexible guidelines with weekly reviews. The tone and structure of the plan should match their motivation style.
The format of the plan (spreadsheet, journal, app, printed calendar) determines how actionable and usable it will be day-to-day.

gold.taskDescription: Create a structured 30-day plan to stop non-essential spending, covering rules, tracking, and motivation strategies.

questions.title: Which spending categories are fully off-limits for you?
questions.description: Identify exactly which types of spending are banned — e.g., takeout, clothing, entertainment, subscriptions — versus what is allowed as a necessity.

questions.title: Are you doing this alone or with others?
questions.description: Determine whether a partner, roommate, or friend is participating, which affects shared expenses, accountability, and rule-setting.

questions.title: When does your 30-day window start?
questions.description: Pin down the start date and flag any events in the period — social occasions, travel, or celebrations — that may need advance planning.

questions.title: What recurring bills or fixed costs stay in place?
questions.description: List unavoidable obligations like rent, utilities, insurance, and existing subscriptions so they can be clearly separated from discretionary spending in the plan.

questions.title: What is the main outcome you want from this challenge?
questions.description: Clarify the primary goal — saving a specific dollar amount, paying down debt, breaking an impulse-spending habit — so the plan can measure the right thing.

questions.title: Do you prefer strict daily rules or flexible weekly guidelines?
questions.description: Understand whether the user thrives with rigid structure and daily check-ins or a looser framework with periodic reviews, to match their motivation style.

questions.title: What format do you want the plan delivered in?
questions.description: Decide on the practical format — a day-by-day calendar, a spreadsheet tracker, a journaling template, or an app-based system — so the output is immediately usable.
